Pontiac Firebird Trans Am Spent Over 40 Years Abandoned in a Closed Dealership, Now It's Finally Out
22 photos
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube
This 1978 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am was traded in at 2,000 miles with a mechanical issue. The dealership shop slapped a band-aid on it and was planning to sell it quickly. However, the dealership closed, and the car remained abandoned at the back of the shop.
1978 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am sat abandoned in a closed dealership in a small town in Georgia. The service manager tried to sell the car, but it never actually made it to the showroom. It just sat in the back, hidden away from the eyes of the customers until the dealership was permanently shut down. Now, Vagner Moleiro of Percepcar USA bought it for $15,000.
The car had been brought in as a trade-in at just 2,000 miles and got a patchwork fix. Then, over the years, it just sat there, untouched, collecting dust instead of miles, and grime that hid away the Trans Am's typical black and gold paint scheme .
The entire lower section is covered in mud, which is a hint that the car wasn't even washed before it entered service over 40 years ago. The cabin is covered in dry mud and debris, like this car spent its entire life on a construction site. Now, power washing reveals a black paint that has gone dull. But clay barring and polishing every inch of the Firebird will work miracles.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube General Motors phased out Hurst Hatches around mid-1978 in favor of its own Fisher T-tops, which were the factory T-top roof style for 1979 T rans Ams . Hurst panels are smaller (roughly 30.25" × 17.5"), leaving about 16 inches of center roof structure between them. Meanwhile, the Fisher panels are larger (about 33.5" × 22.25"), leaving about 6 inches between them.
In 1978, Pontiac rolled out 3,643 Firebird Trans Ams in Black and Gold. Of the 3,643, only 298 units featured the Fisher T-Tops. Of the 298, only 88 of them had the 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) V8 under the hood like this Trans Am, which makes it incredibly rare and definitely worth saving. “I’m not going to be the one who loses one that way,” Vagner says.
Now, 48 years later, the price tag is still dangling from the mirror. He bought for cheap a car that would normally be around $80,000 and can cross the $100,000 mark in top condition. In 1978, a new Pontiac Firebird Trans Am had a base MSRP of $7,135 before any fees or options.
The Black & Gold Special Edition Package (RPO Y82/Y84) was a $1,260 deal at the time, and it included the T-tops, gold cast-aluminum snowflake wheels, black-and-gold striping and decals, and the gold interior accents on the dashboard, steering wheel, and door panels.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube From the moment Vagner parked the car in his shop, Benjamin took over. With the vehicle up on a lift, he inspected the underside with a flashlight. He stopped at the front, where he noticed silicone that did not come from the factory leaking out at the seam of the timing cover, along with a massive oil leak.
Someone had already worked on that area, taking off the distributor cap and marking the rotor and the pulley with chalk to check the timing chain. They had likely suspected the stretched timing chain had jumped a tooth.
Expectedly, the 400-cubic-inch Pontiac W72 V8 is a no-runner. It has been hibernating for roughly four decades, but when it did run, it pumped out 220 horsepower (223 metric horsepower) and 320 pound-feet (434 Newton meters) of torque.
That made the F-body Pontiac Firebird Trans Am flash from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 6.7 seconds on its way to a top speed of 126 mph (203 kph). The Borg-Warner Super T-10 four-speed manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube Vagner is well aware that if the 400 V8 needs a rebuild, it is going to cost him around $6,000. But before he makes any move, he needs to remove all the dust and grease from the engine bay. In the meantime, he does some research and finds out that the model was recalled for fan blade replacement.
Flexible cooling fans that equipped the 1978 Firebird Trans Am were designed with thinner steel blades that flattened out at highway speeds to reduce drag and save fuel. Over time, normal engine vibration and flexing caused metal fatigue and hairline stress cracks around the central hub or rivets, which could allow a blade to break off while the engine was running.
Benjamin takes the front end apart to access the internals. Removing the cover reveals that three plastic teeth from the aluminum timing gear were missing. No wonder this car was parked and never driven again. The mechanic realizes that someone at the service shop had slapped on a cheap replacement chain simply to get the Trans Am out the door.
So from this moment on, Benjamin can either replace the chain and the gears for around $130 or rebuild the entire front assembly, including a new water pump and timing cover, for about $800. He will also need to work on the brakes and replace the brake fluid, which has gone the color of coffee after sitting for so long in the reservoir. Expectedly, the engine oil has gone black and thick. No surprise there, either.
Photo: Percepcar USA | YouTube After hours of hard work, the V8 roars back to life and sounds like it longed for the road. " It stays with me until it drives the miles that the dealership never drove, " says Vagner. He paid just $15,000 to take it home. On the collector market, Black & Gold Special Editions (Y82/Y84) average $68,000 to $85,000.
